tips: Start with Hosea's marriage (chapters 1–3). God tells him to marry Gomer, who is unfaithful, so that his own heartbreak becomes a living picture of Israel's unfaithfulness to God.
Watch for the names of Hosea's children, Lo-ruhamah ("not pitied") and Lo-ammi ("not my people"), and how God promises to reverse them (Hosea 1:6–10; 2:23).
Read chapter 11 as the emotional center of the book. God speaks like a father who taught his child to walk and cannot give him up.

looksBack.title: The last days of the northern kingdom
looksBack.text: Hosea preaches to Israel in the decades before Assyria conquers it, the period of 2 Kings 14–17.

looksBack.title: Out of Egypt
looksBack.text: Hosea reminds Israel of the exodus: "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt" (Hosea 11:1).

looksAhead.title: Called out of Egypt
looksAhead.text: Matthew applies Hosea 11:1 to Jesus returning from Egypt as a child (Matthew 2:15).

looksAhead.title: Not my people
looksAhead.text: Paul and Peter apply the reversal of "not my people" to Gentiles welcomed into God's people (Romans 9:25–26; 1 Peter 2:10).

looksAhead.title: Mercy, not sacrifice
looksAhead.text: Jesus twice quotes Hosea 6:6: "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice" (Matthew 9:13; 12:7).

tips: Begin with the disaster Joel describes: a locust plague and drought (chapter 1). He uses this real catastrophe as a warning of a greater one, "the day of the LORD."
Notice the turn at Joel 2:12–13, "rend your heart, and not your garments." God calls for genuine repentance and describes himself as "gracious and merciful."
Read the second half of the book as God's answer: restoration of what the locusts destroyed (Joel 2:25) and the promise to pour out his Spirit on all people.

looksBack.title: God's name revealed
looksBack.text: Joel's description of God as "gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness" (Joel 2:13) echoes what God proclaimed to Moses at Sinai (Exodus 34:6).

looksAhead.title: Pentecost
looksAhead.text: Peter explains the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost by quoting Joel 2:28–32: "this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel" (Acts 2:16–21).

looksAhead.title: Call on the name of the Lord
looksAhead.text: Paul quotes Joel 2:32 to show the gospel is for everyone: "whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved" (Romans 10:13).

tips: Notice the clever opening (chapters 1–2). Amos condemns Israel's neighbors one by one, drawing his listeners in, and then turns the same judgment on Israel itself.
Read it against a time of prosperity. Israel was wealthy and religious, but Amos exposes how the rich crushed the poor and how worship had become empty.
Remember the book's key line: "let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream" (Amos 5:24). God cares about justice as much as worship.

looksBack.title: Jeroboam's golden calves
looksBack.text: Amos preaches at Bethel (Amos 7:10–13), the shrine where Jeroboam had set up a golden calf when the kingdom divided (1 Kings 12:28–29).

looksAhead.title: David's fallen tent
looksAhead.text: At the Jerusalem council, James quotes Amos 9:11–12 to show that God planned to include the Gentiles (Acts 15:13–17).

looksAhead.title: Stephen's sermon
looksAhead.text: Stephen quotes Amos 5:25–27 in his speech about Israel's history of idolatry (Acts 7:42–43).

tips: Learn the background first. Edom was descended from Esau, Jacob's brother, so its gloating over Jerusalem's fall was a betrayal within the family (Obadiah 1:10–12).
Read it in one sitting—it is a single chapter. The first part announces Edom's fall for its pride; the second looks to "the day of the LORD" and Israel's restoration.
Notice the final line, "the kingdom shall be the LORD's" (Obadiah 1:21). The book is less about Edom than about God's justice and his coming reign.

looksBack.title: Jacob and Esau
looksBack.text: The conflict reaches back to the twins who struggled in Rebekah's womb (Genesis 25:22–23) and to Esau's anger at Jacob (Genesis 27:41).

looksAhead.title: Edom's end
looksAhead.text: Malachi 1:2–4 describes Edom already laid waste, and Paul cites the choice of Jacob over Esau in Romans 9:10–13.

tips: Read it as a story with a surprise ending. The book closes with God's question to Jonah (Jonah 4:11), leaving the reader to answer it.
Notice that the pagans in the story—the sailors and the people of Nineveh—respond to God better than God's own prophet does.
Read Jonah's prayer from inside the fish (chapter 2) alongside his angry prayer in chapter 4. He celebrates mercy for himself but resents it for his enemies.

looksBack.title: A prophet in Kings
looksBack.text: Jonah son of Amittai is mentioned in 2 Kings 14:25 as a prophet who foretold Israel's expansion under Jeroboam II.

looksBack.title: The gracious God
looksBack.text: Jonah complains that God is "gracious" and "merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness" (Jonah 4:2), quoting God's own self-description in Exodus 34:6.

looksAhead.title: The sign of Jonah
looksAhead.text: Jesus compares his three days in the tomb to Jonah's three days in the fish, and the repentance of Nineveh to his own hearers' unbelief (Matthew 12:39–41).

tips: Follow the book's rhythm of judgment and hope. Each of its three sections opens with "Hear" (Micah 1:2; 3:1; 6:1) and moves from judgment to promise.
Notice that Micah, a man from the countryside, targets the leaders of the capital cities: corrupt rulers, false prophets, and greedy landowners.
Memorize the book's summary of true religion: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God" (Micah 6:8).

looksBack.title: Isaiah's contemporary
looksBack.text: Micah prophesies at the same time as Isaiah, and Micah 4:1–3 closely matches Isaiah 2:2–4.

looksAhead.title: Born in Bethlehem
looksAhead.text: The chief priests answer Herod with Micah 5:2: the ruler of Israel would come from Bethlehem (Matthew 2:4–6).

looksAhead.title: A family divided
looksAhead.text: Jesus echoes Micah 7:6 when he says a man's foes will be those of his own household (Matthew 10:35–36).

tips: Read it as a sequel to Jonah. About a century after Nineveh repented, the city has returned to cruelty, and Nahum announces its fall.
Notice how the book begins with who God is (Nahum 1:2–8): he is jealous and avenging, yet "slow to anger" and "a strong hold in the day of trouble." Both truths matter.
Remember the original audience. For Judah, long oppressed by Assyria, Nahum's message was good news (Nahum 1:15).

looksBack.title: Nineveh in Jonah
looksBack.text: Jonah's message brought Nineveh to repentance (Jonah 3:5–10); Nahum shows that repentance did not last.

looksBack.title: Assyria's cruelty
looksBack.text: Assyria had destroyed the northern kingdom (2 Kings 17:5–6) and threatened Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:13–19:37).

looksAhead.title: Beautiful feet
looksAhead.text: Nahum's image of a messenger bringing good tidings (Nahum 1:15; compare Isaiah 52:7) is applied to preachers of the gospel in Romans 10:15.

looksAhead.title: The fall of proud cities
looksAhead.text: Revelation's lament over fallen Babylon (Revelation 18) echoes the prophets' oracles against proud cities like Nineveh.

tips: Read it as a conversation. Habakkuk complains to God (Habakkuk 1:2–4), God answers, Habakkuk complains again (1:12–2:1), and God answers again.
Notice that the prophet's questions are honest: why does God allow injustice, and how can he use an even more wicked nation to punish it? The book shows it is right to bring hard questions to God.
End with the prayer of chapter 3. Habakkuk resolves to rejoice in God even if the fig tree does not blossom and the fields yield no food (Habakkuk 3:17–18).

looksBack.title: On the eve of exile
looksBack.text: Habakkuk speaks as Babylon rises, shortly before the invasions of 2 Kings 24.

looksAhead.title: The just shall live by faith
looksAhead.text: Habakkuk 2:4 is quoted three times in the New Testament: "The just shall live by faith" (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11; Hebrews 10:38).

looksAhead.title: The earth filled with God's glory
looksAhead.text: The promise that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD (Habakkuk 2:14) looks ahead to the new creation of Revelation 21–22.

tips: Focus on the book's main theme, the day of the LORD. It is described with overwhelming images of darkness and destruction (Zephaniah 1:14–18).
Notice the wide scope: judgment on Judah, then on the surrounding nations, then on Jerusalem again, before a promise of restoration.
Read the ending slowly. Zephaniah 3:17 pictures God rejoicing over his people "with singing"—a striking reversal after the warnings of judgment.

looksBack.title: Before Josiah's reform
looksBack.text: Zephaniah preaches in the days of Josiah (Zephaniah 1:1), and his attack on idol worship fits the conditions Josiah's reform addressed (2 Kings 23:4–14).

looksAhead.title: The day of the Lord
looksAhead.text: The New Testament continues Zephaniah's theme of the coming day of the Lord (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10).

looksAhead.title: A gathered people
looksAhead.text: Zephaniah's vision of nations calling on the LORD with a pure language (Zephaniah 3:9) is often linked to the reversal of Babel at Pentecost (Acts 2:5–11).

tips: Read it against Ezra 1–6. The exiles had returned and laid the temple's foundation but then stopped building for about sixteen years.
Notice the repeated call, "Consider your ways" (Haggai 1:5, 7). The people had time to build their own paneled houses but not God's house.

Watch for the encouragement in chapter 2. Those who remember Solomon's temple are disappointed, but God promises that "the glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former" (Haggai 2:9).

looksBack.title: The stalled temple
looksBack.text: Ezra records that Haggai and Zechariah stirred the people to rebuild (Ezra 5:1–2), and the temple was finished in 515 BC (Ezra 6:14–15).

looksAhead.title: Shaking the heavens
looksAhead.text: Hebrews 12:26–28 quotes Haggai 2:6 to describe a kingdom "which cannot be moved."

looksAhead.title: Zerubbabel the signet
looksAhead.text: God's promise to make Zerubbabel like a signet ring (Haggai 2:23) renews the hope for David's line; Zerubbabel appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:12–13).

tips: Read it in two parts. Chapters 1–8 contain eight night visions and messages encouraging the temple builders; chapters 9–14 are undated oracles about the coming king and the final day of the LORD.
Don't get lost in the visions' details. Each one ends with a clear message, such as "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6).
Watch for the coming king in chapters 9–14: humble and riding on a donkey, betrayed for thirty pieces of silver, and pierced.

looksBack.title: Rebuilding the temple
looksBack.text: Zechariah encourages the same builders as Haggai (Ezra 5:1; 6:14); the high priest Joshua and the governor Zerubbabel appear in his visions (Zechariah 3–4).

looksAhead.title: The king on a donkey
looksAhead.text: Jesus' entry into Jerusalem fulfills Zechariah 9:9 (Matthew 21:4–5; John 12:14–15).

looksAhead.title: Thirty pieces of silver
looksAhead.text: Judas's price and the potter's field (Matthew 26:15; 27:9–10) recall Zechariah 11:12–13.

looksAhead.title: The pierced one
looksAhead.text: John cites Zechariah 12:10, "they shall look upon me whom they have pierced," at the crucifixion (John 19:37) and at Christ's return (Revelation 1:7).

tips: Read it as a series of six disputes. Each one follows the same pattern: God makes a claim, the people object with "Wherein…?", and God answers (for example Malachi 1:2, 6; 2:17; 3:7–8).
Notice the setting. The temple has been rebuilt, but the people and priests have grown careless—offering blemished animals, breaking marriages, and withholding tithes.
Read the ending as a doorway. The last words of the Old Testament promise a messenger to prepare the way and the return of Elijah before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5–6).

looksBack.title: Nehemiah's reforms
looksBack.text: Malachi confronts the same failures that Nehemiah faced after the walls were rebuilt (Nehemiah 13:10–29).

looksBack.title: Remember the law of Moses
looksBack.text: The book's final charge is to "Remember ye the law of Moses my servant" (Malachi 4:4), pointing back to Sinai.

looksAhead.title: The messenger
looksAhead.text: The Gospels identify John the Baptist as the messenger of Malachi 3:1 (Mark 1:2; Matthew 11:10).

looksAhead.title: Elijah who was to come
looksAhead.text: The angel says John will go before the Lord "in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children" (Luke 1:17; Malachi 4:6).
